text:
alex: Heads up — we just had another burst of GPU node churn in us-west2. ~8 GPU nodes deleted in the last 20m while batch jobs were finishing, pods with local emptyDir kept blocking drains. Anyone tracking this?

maya: Saw it too. Alerts show scale-down triggered roughly 6m after pods went to Completed/Terminating. We set --scale-down-unneeded-time=10m last month to be aggressive; might be too aggressive for GPU batches and slow egress.

ben: Two quick suspects: pods with local storage/daemonsets and PDBs. Also kube-probe flaps can mark nodes unready and CA treats them differently. Check for pods missing "cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict" annotation and any long terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

sam: Proposal for an experiment (small canary in us-west2 only): relax a few flags, add bulk-delete guard, and switch expander. Example flags for the canary autoscaler deployment:

```
--expander=least-waste
--scale-down-unneeded-time=15m
--scale-down-unready-time=20m
--scale-down-utilization-threshold=0.5
--max-empty-bulk-delete=5
--balance-similar-node-groups=true
```

sam: Rationale: least-waste should prefer deleting nodes with most free capacity vs strictly binpack, increasing unneeded/unready windows avoids deleting nodes while pods are terminating or network egress is slow, and bulk-delete cap prevents mass simultaneous node removals.

maya: +1 on the bulk-delete cap. Also we should hunt for slow finalizers/egress issues — yesterday a long S3 upload on completion kept a pod terminating for >8m, blocking node deletion. Maybe add a pre-drain hook for batch jobs to signal when uploads are done.

ben: Another operational pattern: tag batch workloads with an annotation to opt them into a longer safety window. We could add a small controller that sets an internal annotation like "infra.redwood/scale-down-hold" for pods labeled "workload=batch" and CA can respect that via a custom check before drain (or we implement a webhook that temporarily adds the "cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict" flag later). Less invasive than bumping global timeouts cluster-wide.

alex: What's the cost tradeoff if we bump from 10m to 15m? Quick back-of-envelope: average GPU node $2.40/hr -> extra 5m/node ~ $0.20 per node per incident. If this prevents repeated re-provisioning and warm-up penalties it's probably net savings. But need numbers.

sam: Let's run a 48h canary in us-west2 with those flags and collect: node churn rate, avg pod termination times, wasted vCPU/GPU time, and billing delta. If it looks good, roll to other regions with lower-cost settings.

ops-bot: deploy-bot: autoscaler-canary (us-west2) updated with new flags at 2026-03-18T16:30:10Z — watching.

maya: One last note — we might also enable "scale-down-delay-after-add" to prevent nodes added for burst from being removed immediately if they don't get workload. Set to 10m for the canary.

alex: Cool. Sam, can you open a short runbook for the canary with rollback steps (patch revert command + threshold for abort)? If we hit >10% increase in cost or >2x pod restarts rollback immediately.

sam: Will do. I'll post the patch + metrics dashboard link in this thread once it's up.

ben: Also add a grep command in the runbook to find blocking pods: `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.annotations."cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict" != "true") | {ns: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, grace: .spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds}'`

alex: Thanks — leaning to conservative change. Let's keep close watch.
